identification.summary: Microsoft's umbrella name for multiple threat actors associated with remote access or information-stealing malware that is distributed through phishing, search engine optimization (SEO) or malvertising [S1]. It is a catch-all cluster label, not a single actor [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: The best-documented activity under the label was detected by Microsoft in early December 2024 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft's mapping file lists Storm-0408 as a 'group in development' with no other vendor names [S2]. Do not merge with Storm-2477, which Microsoft separately tracks as the developer and operator of the Lumma Stealer malware-as-a-service offering [S4]; Storm-0408's December 2024 campaign delivered Lumma as one payload [S1]. Silobreaker's page URL suggests an April 2021 weekly summary while its text describes the December 2024 campaign, so that source was not used.

attribution.basis: Microsoft does not name a specific group or country for the Storm-0408 activity; it describes the operators only as actors using remote access or information-stealing malware under the umbrella name [S1]. Press coverage likewise presents Storm-0408 as a catch-all label rather than a single actor [S3]. No state sponsorship is asserted in the sources gathered.

objectives: Opportunistic information theft: the December 2024 campaign collected browser credentials and cookies, documents and cryptocurrency wallet data, and installed NetSupport RAT for remote control [S1].

targeting.notes: Microsoft describes the December 2024 campaign as opportunistic, affecting nearly one million devices globally across consumer and enterprise systems in many industries [S1]. Victims were reached through illegal streaming sites [S1].

capabilities.summary: Malvertising redirectors embedded in iframes on illegal streaming sites led through four to five layers of redirection, sometimes via a malware or tech-support scam site, to payloads hosted mainly on GitHub, with one payload each on Discord and Dropbox [S1]. First-stage droppers were signed with certificates (twelve identified and revoked) and bundled legitimate DLLs and archives [S1]. Later stages performed system discovery with Base64-encoded exfiltration to C2 IPs, searched for security software, downloaded NetSupport RAT, and used AutoIt-based components for browser remote debugging, DPAPI decryption and credential-file access [S1]. A final PowerShell stage added Microsoft Defender exclusion paths [S1]. Final payloads were mostly Lumma Stealer or an updated Doenerium [S1]. Living-off-the-land binaries (PowerShell, MSBuild.exe, RegAsm.exe) were used for C2 and exfiltration, with persistence through Run keys, Startup-folder shortcuts and scheduled tasks, plus process injection and disabled TLS settings [S1].

campaigns.name: Malvertising campaign delivering infostealers via GitHub
campaigns.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected the campaign in early December 2024. It redirected users from illegal streaming sites to GitHub-hosted droppers that led to Lumma Stealer or Doenerium and often NetSupport RAT, affecting nearly one million devices [S1]. GitHub took down the malicious repositories [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published its analysis, hunting queries, detections and IOC tables for the campaign on 6 March 2025 [S1]. Trade press repeated the roughly one-million-device figure [S3].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed set of actors distributing remote access or information-stealing malware under an umbrella label; no group or country named [S1].
diamond.capability: Malvertising redirect chains, signed multi-stage droppers, Lumma Stealer, Doenerium, NetSupport RAT, AutoIt components, PowerShell and LOLBAS abuse [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Malvertising redirectors on illegal streaming sites, intermediate redirect sites, GitHub repositories (main), Discord and Dropbox hosting, and C2 IP addresses; IOC tables are in Microsoft's post [S1].
diamond.victim: Consumer and enterprise devices across many industries worldwide, about one million devices [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, Chromium and Firefox browser credential stores, DPAPI, Defender exclusions, and trusted developer and file-sharing platforms (GitHub, Discord, Dropbox) used for payload hosting [S1].

gaps: No sponsor, nationality or motive beyond opportunistic theft is stated in the sources gathered [S1].
Storm-0408 is an umbrella label; which actors fall under it and what other campaigns Microsoft assigns to it were not found in public sources beyond the December 2024 campaign.
Whether the stolen data fed ransomware or initial-access brokerage downstream is not stated in the sources gathered.
The Microsoft naming mapping lists no aliases and an unspecified group-in-development status [S2]; overlap with other vendor clusters is unknown.

The Silobreaker summary and the Hacker News article could not be opened (host not reachable); the Hacker News and SecurityWeek items were seen only as search results [S3]. Microsoft's Lumma post does not mention Storm-0408 [S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the user endpoint and browser, where credentials and cookies are stored, and trusted hosting platforms (GitHub, Dropbox, Discord) that the actors abuse [S1]. STEP 2: The actors are opportunistic and non-selective, reaching consumer and enterprise devices alike through illegal streaming sites [S1]. Personnel using personal devices or unapproved streaming sites are exposed. STEP 3: The pattern is malvertising redirect, signed dropper from GitHub, discovery, NetSupport RAT and stealer, then Defender exclusions [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic infostealing that harvests credentials and session cookies from any reachable device, including those of DoD-affiliated personnel on personal systems. MDCOA is that stolen access being reused against cleared or contractor accounts; the sources do not show this occurring. Candidate indicators from Microsoft: Defender exclusion path changes, unexpected NetSupport installs, renamed AutoIt binaries, browser remote debugging use and the listed C2 IPs and certificate serial numbers [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track credential and cookie theft exposure for personnel and contractor accounts, and ingest the IOCs in Microsoft's post [S1]. (2) Authorities: blocking streaming and file-hosting domains, and restricting RMM tools with AppLocker, are network and endpoint owner actions that Microsoft lists as mitigations [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce phishing-resistant MFA and session-token revocation so stolen cookies do not give access [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with the command's cyber defenders and report GitHub-hosted malware to the platform operator, which took down the repositories in this case [S1].
